issues.legal_issue: A tenant’s statutory option to purchase demised land in an ejectment proceeding is a limited privilege, not an absolute right.
material_facts: A tenant facing ejectment sought an order directing the landlord to sell the demised land under the statutory tenant-protection scheme.
The lower courts rejected the purchase applications, and the issue was considered in appeals from those decisions.
issues.conclusion: The statutory provision gives a tenant a privilege to seek a conveyance of only the land necessary for convenient enjoyment; the court may grant or refuse that relief on the facts of the case.
issues.legal_principle: Section 9 of the Tamil Nadu City Tenants’ Protection Act, 1921 creates a statutory right to seek purchase through the court, but does not create an interest in the property or an absolute entitlement to purchase. The court has discretion to grant or refuse relief. The Court relied on S.M. Transport (P) Ltd. v. Sankaraswamingal Mutt, [1963] Supp. 1 SCR 282, which held that the statutory right to purchase does not itself create a property right.

predicates.tenant_seeks_purchase_in_ejectment_case: A tenant facing an ejectment proceeding sought an order requiring the landlord to sell the demised land.

issues.definition: When a tenant seeks purchase of demised land in an ejectment proceeding, the tenant has a limited, discretionary purchase right rather than an absolute entitlement.

issues.legal_issue: A tenant who does not occupy or need the land and buildings for residence or business is not entitled to purchase the land for convenient enjoyment.
material_facts: The original business on the demised land had ceased.
The courts found that the tenants were not occupying the land or buildings or carrying on business there, while sub-tenants had occupied the land and buildings for years.
Only a small portion was used to keep account books, and the tenants did not require any portion of the land for convenient enjoyment of the buildings.
issues.conclusion: The tenants did not require the land for convenient enjoyment, so it would be inequitable to direct the landlords to sell it to them; the purchase applications were properly rejected.
issues.legal_principle: Under sections 3 and 9 of the Tamil Nadu City Tenants’ Protection Act, 1921, the court must determine the minimum extent of land necessary for the tenant’s convenient enjoyment, taking account of the land, the buildings, and the tenant’s need. The inquiry presupposes that the tenant occupies the land and buildings for residence or business and would be adversely affected by eviction. If the tenant does not require any part of the land, the court may reject the purchase application. The statutory purchase privilege is equitable and is not intended to let a tenant who has no such need enrich itself at the landlord’s expense. S.M. Transport (P) Ltd. v. Sankaraswamingal Mutt, [1963] Supp. 1 SCR 282, was also relied on for the limited nature of the statutory right.

rule.if: tenant_seeks_purchase_in_ejectment_case and tenant_not_in_occupation and tenant_not_using_property_for_residence_or_business and subtenants_occupy_property

predicates.tenant_seeks_purchase_in_ejectment_case: A tenant facing an ejectment proceeding sought an order requiring the landlord to sell the demised land.
predicates.tenant_not_in_occupation: The tenant was not occupying the demised land or the buildings on it.
predicates.tenant_not_using_property_for_residence_: The tenant was not using the land or buildings for residence or carrying on business there.
predicates.subtenants_occupy_property: Sub-tenants were occupying the demised land and buildings.

issues.definition: When a tenant seeking purchase in an ejectment proceeding is not in occupation or using the property for residence or business, and sub-tenants occupy it, purchase relief may be refused.
